title: I stopped texting first and realized I have exactly zero friendships.
content: Three weeks ago I decided I wasn't going to initiate with anyone. Not a single text. Not a meme or a 'long time' or a 'how are you.' I just stopped. Nobody has reached out. Not one person. I'm sitting with this information and I genuinely don't know what to do with it.

replies.content: you just accidentally ran the most brutal friendship audit known to man
I did this exact thing two years ago. sat with the same silence. it broke me open in a way I actually needed
adult friendships run on initiative. the person who initiates more holds the relationship together. remove them and it collapses.
three weeks of silence is a full personality diagnosis on everyone in your contact list
zero is a real number and it's telling you something important
before anything else — are you okay? that kind of silence hits hard
what you're mourning isn't the silence. it's the version of closeness you thought you had
don't interpret yet. just collect the data for now
I mean... are you also texting back quickly when they do reach out? passive friendship cuts both ways
the hard part is you found out. a lot of people never find out and just keep investing in nothing
and honestly the people defending the 'they're just busy' angle are coping hard
what I found was that two people eventually reached out. those are the two I still talk to
this isn't a moral failing on their end. it's just how most people operate passively in relationships
the people in the comments saying 'they might just be busy' babe it's been THREE WEEKS
I'm not going to sugarcoat it — this hurts because it's meant to hurt. let it
people genuinely don't notice until you're gone. it's not always malice, it's just obliviousness
most friendships are agreements to mutually maintain a feeling. you were maintaining alone
when you're ready, pick the two or three who matter most. re-initiate once and see what happens
three weeks might just be a bad month for all of them simultaneously. it does happen
this is the cleared ground you needed to build something better on
three weeks of silence from people who call you a close friend is genuinely damning
the others weren't bad people. they were just coasting on my effort and had no idea they were doing it
the question now is what do you actually do with this information
I feel like this experiment should be mandatory at 25. save everyone years of confusion
the people defending them haven't tried this themselves. everyone thinks they're the exception until they're not
I wonder if any of them would be shocked to learn this. some probably genuinely would be
the silence isn't an absence of caring necessarily. it's an absence of practice. they never built the muscle
the ones worth keeping will notice the difference when you reach back out. the others won't
I'm not defending the silence but 'no one texted me first' isn't always the full picture
the right friendships are still out there. this just makes space for them to actually be seen
the fact that this is making some people uncomfortable in the comments is telling honestly
I think what hurt most was realizing I'd been performing closeness for years without realizing it
you can re-initiate with the ones that matter. you just know now it'll always be you. decide if that's okay
the audacity of having a 'bestie' who hasn't texted in 21 days is a special kind of thing
at least you're not finding out at 45. you have real time to build something different
reach out to the one or two you actually care about. not as accusation. just honesty
the question beneath this is: what kind of person do you want to be in friendships going forward
join something — a class, a team, a regular group — and build from shared context. it's how it actually works
some people show friendship very differently. not everyone communicates through texts specifically
knowing who actually shows up is worth the pain of finding out who doesn't
you learned something most people spend decades avoiding. that's a strange gift
two years later the circle is smaller but every person in it actually shows up. that trade was worth it
or use this as the push to build differently with new people. both paths are completely valid
anyway you have us now. this thread counts as a friendship. I'm initiating. hi.
the silence wasn't them failing you. it was information. the kind you needed to receive
sometimes the friendship is still worth saving even if you have to be the one who keeps saving it
there is something clarifying about grief. you're clearer now than you were a month ago. sit with that
give it one more month. truly. then decide. grief distorts timelines
I'd genuinely be curious what they'd say if you told them this. probably not what you're expecting
you didn't lose anything you actually had. you gained clarity. that's a different kind of thing entirely

title: My situationship of 8 months just posted a picture with someone new. I don't have the right to be hurt. But I am.
content: We never put a label on it. That was 'my choice too' apparently. I'm staring at this photo and I feel sick. I can't even be angry because I knew the rules going in. The worst part is I think I loved him. Past tense. He's already moved on.

replies.content: 8 months is a relationship. they just didn't give it the word
the labeling conversation was never really about labels. it was about whether he was willing to choose you
8 months, no label, already got a photoshoot with someone new. the audacity is a spectator sport
I spent 11 months in something like this. finding out the way you did is a specific kind of brutal
he had 8 months to define this. he chose not to. that choice was about him, not you
he knew exactly what he was doing for 8 months and posted that photo knowing you'd probably see it
I know this hurts but you genuinely agreed to the no-label arrangement at some point
be gentle with yourself right now. this is real pain regardless of what the label was
I've watched people spend years in arrangements like this waiting for the person to finally choose them. they rarely do
eight months of almost. that's what hurts. not the absence of a word but the presence of almost everything
and the fact that you're calling it a situationship means he already had power over the framing
people who won't commit to a title are often people who are hedging. that's the honest read
the way he probably told himself he was 'being honest' the whole time is genuinely the funniest lie
what hurt me most wasn't the person. it was having to grieve quietly because 'we weren't even together'
the 'no label by mutual agreement' thing usually means one person wanted a label and was talked out of it
the 'we never labeled it' conversation is specifically designed to neutralize your right to be upset later
I'm not saying that makes it painless. I'm saying you have information now about what you'll accept next time
you don't have to figure out what it all means today. just get through today first
the pain you feel is proportional to what you gave. you gave a lot. honor that
you named it a situationship to make it smaller. it wasn't smaller. it was just unnamed
the 'my choice too' line they fed you was designed to make you complicit in your own pain
you didn't break any rules. the rules were designed to protect him, not you
the algorithm really said 'here, receive this content' and delivered it straight to your feed. absolutely rude
I remember staring at a similar photo and doing math. how long. how long did he know her while we were still happening
the hurt is valid. the situation was not fair to you. both things are true at the same time
and now someone will say 'you knew the rules' as if those rules were ever fair to begin with
was there a moment where you could have pushed for clarity and didn't? not blame. just growth material
the people saying you 'knew the rules' are missing that knowing a rule doesn't stop it from hurting
he didn't do anything wrong by the letter of the agreement. but the spirit of it was never equal
grief that has no label is grief that has to be carried alone. that's the cruelest part of all this
you're allowed to be hurt. you're allowed to be angry. you gave 8 months of your actual life
what you're feeling is legitimate grief from a legitimate loss. the informality doesn't change the reality
I need everyone who has been in a situationship for more than 3 months to unionize immediately
what helped me was writing everything I felt without sending it. the relationship I deserved to have existed on paper
this doesn't mean the next person will do this. it means this person was willing to. that's his specific character
the picture might have been intentional. not saying that to hurt you. saying it because you should know it's possible
he might not have known how deep you were in. people in these situations often convince themselves the other is equally unbothered
it's okay to reach out to someone you trust and just say 'I'm not okay.' you don't have to explain everything
you'll look back knowing the version of you who accepted this was doing the best she could with what she knew then
somewhere in you is the girl who knew she deserved a full answer. she was right the whole time
grieve it properly. don't minimize it because he convinced you it wasn't real. it was real to you
you loved someone. that's not embarrassing. it's just true and it deserves to be acknowledged
okay but are we going to acknowledge that 'my choice too' is one of the most gaslit sentences in the English language
you're going to be okay. not today. but the version of you on the other side of this is going to be so clear
take the full time you need. don't let anyone tell you this doesn't count because it didn't have a name
you are not the problem in this story. the setup was designed for you to lose from the very start
the picture might not be what it looks like. or it might. you're building a story on one image
when you're ready, think about what you'd want said up front next time. that clarity is what you're building now
the next relationship will have a different quality. you'll know what to ask for. that knowledge is not nothing
let yourself mourn this one fully. unnamed things deserve real funerals too

title: I matched with my colleague on a dating app. We both unmatched without saying a word. Every meeting since has been unbearable.
content: It's been six weeks. We've had four team calls and one all-hands. We both pretend with such commitment that it's almost impressive. The worst part is I think I would have said yes. I'll never know if he would have. I just have to sit at 9am standups forever now.

replies.content: the mutual unmatch is a legally binding contract. neither party may speak of this. ever.
I once matched with someone from my office and we ALSO both unmatched immediately. we see each other monthly. it's magnificent
he swiped right on you. that's information your brain has now and it will never leave
the mutual unmatch was the correct call. clean, professional, dignified. well done actually
you both swiped right. sit with that for a second before anything else
okay but what made you swipe right on him in the first place? like what did you actually see
you're both adults who handled an awkward situation as gracefully as you possibly could. give yourself credit
why does this have to be unbearable? you're both adults. nothing actually happened.
don't do anything right now. just let time do the work. brains habituate faster than we expect
at 2am I've been thinking about all the parallel versions of this where one of you said something
the way you both just looked at the screen and decided 'nope, chaos, unmatch' simultaneously
the unspoken pact is a real thing. it forms instantaneously and both parties understand it without speaking
and YOU swiped right on him. we're not glossing over that part of the story
the awkwardness exists only because you're both aware of it. commit to ignoring it and it actually fades
the whole 'unbearable standups' thing is entirely in your head and I mean that genuinely and kindly
and when you saw the match notification what was your first feeling before the panic set in
the standups feel unbearable now but feelings normalize faster than we expect when we stop feeding them
I feel like people really underestimate how fast 'awkward thing' becomes 'background thing' when you're professional
in a month the physiological awkwardness response fades significantly. give it real time before any action
there's a whole life that almost started in that notification screen and now it's just a thing you carry alone
six weeks and four meetings in and you're both COMMITTED to this bit and honestly I respect it deeply
what kills me is you'll never know if he was relieved or disappointed when he saw it was you
the six weeks of professional commitment to pretending is genuinely impressive. most people crack before week two
people date colleagues all the time. you both read the situation and noped out. that's actually good judgment
he's probably not thinking about it as much as you are. men are like that. infuriating but also useful
do you think he recognised you immediately or did it take a second before it clicked
the mutual decision not to address it is actually a shared act of protection for both of you
the unbearable standups are a choice. you're choosing to make it weird in your own head every morning
the only actual risk is if one of you is the other's direct manager. are you? that changes everything
the strangest intimacy is knowing something about someone that they know you know and you both say absolutely nothing
imagine if one of you just said 'so.' in a meeting. the power that single word would hold
there's a kind of bond in the shared awkwardness though. you have a secret together even if you never say it
one of you is going to slip eventually. a look that lasts half a second too long. just wait
in six months this will be a funny story you don't tell anyone because you still work together
the longer you treat it as A Thing the more of a thing it becomes. it's only real if you keep making it real
what would you actually say if one of you broke the silence? have you thought about the words
a very casual 'this is a funny coincidence' in a low-stakes moment could honestly clear the air
if you find him attractive and he swiped right on you... why is this definitely a closed door
keep being excellent at your job. professional excellence is the best thing you can put between you and this
standups at 9am are such a specific hell when your brain is holding something it can't put down
you will tell this story at his wedding or yours or nobody's. either way it's a great story
years from now one of you will leave the company and only then will you finally be able to laugh about it
what's the actual worst case if one of you just acknowledged it? probably less bad than 20 more years of this
just keep being completely normal at every meeting. normalcy compounds over time. in a year this is genuinely nothing
it was an app. you swiped. you unmatched. the meeting is in 20 minutes. go wash your face.
I just want to know if you think there was something there or if it was purely circumstantial swiping
you don't have to fix this. sometimes things just become part of the background noise of working with someone
I've dated a colleague. it required communication and maturity but it wasn't the disaster everyone warns about
if it genuinely affects your ability to work together, a light joke that acknowledges it is better than sustained silence
one day it'll just be a funny thing you tell someone new and you won't remember why it felt so enormous

title: My best friend told me something in confidence 3 years ago. I still can't look at her the same.
content: She told me about something she did. Not illegal. Not unforgivable. But something that showed me who she is when no one's watching. I've never told a soul. I never will. But I've been quietly grieving the version of her I thought I knew ever since. She has no idea. We still hang out every week.

replies.content: you're grieving an image. the person is still there. the image was always incomplete
I've held secrets like this for twenty years. you never fully go back. you just find a different way forward
you carrying this alone for three years while still showing up every week is actually a form of love
three years is a long time to carry someone else's truth without being able to set it down
you know her better than almost anyone now. that's not a curse. it's just the full picture
a friend told me something twelve years ago that I haven't been able to fully shake. I understand exactly this weight
you've been quietly judging her for three years without telling her. is that the friend you want to be
what kind of thing makes someone grieve a friendship from the inside while still maintaining it from the outside
you're protecting her from consequences she doesn't even know she's avoiding
the worst kind of loneliness is knowing something about someone that you can never unknow
the thing she told you revealed her. but revelation is not condemnation
the grief you're feeling is appropriate. something did change. but changed doesn't mean broken
she didn't lose you. you chose not to let her. I think that matters more than you realize
the fact that it was 'not illegal, not unforgivable' means the friendship has a foundation if you let it
the friendship that survives seeing the real thing is actually the stronger one. not the easier one. the stronger one.
what I've learned is the secret doesn't go away but your relationship with it can change over time
everyone has something they've done that would shift how someone sees them if they knew. everyone.
do you think she knows it changed you? people who share those things sometimes sense the shift afterward
the 'I'll never tell anyone' is a loyalty she didn't earn if it's costing you this much personally
you're holding a version of her that she doesn't know you're holding. every week you carry it to her door
the question isn't whether you can love her knowing this. it's whether you can love the fuller, real version
she trusted you with it because somewhere she knew you could hold it. that's its own significant thing
is there any version of this where you could tell her it shifted something? not to relitigate. just to be honest
you made a choice every week for three years to keep showing up. that means you still want this friendship
the part you're not saying is whether it changed how you trust her or just how you see her. those are different things
I found that naming it to myself — not to her, just to me — helped. 'this happened. I know it. I'm still here.'
the fact that you're still showing up every week suggests you've already decided you're staying. the grief is just the adjustment period
has she ever referenced it again or is it completely unacknowledged between both of you
three years of suppressing this is doing its own damage. not to her. to you specifically
grief for the living is quieter than the other kind. harder to justify. harder to set down.
most friendships survive on a curated selection of truth. you got more than the curation and now you're adjusting
the question at year three is whether the friendship you have now is still actually worth having
not as accusation. just as truth. 'I've been carrying something and it's become heavy.' friendships can hold that
the version of her you're grieving was never fully real anyway. people are more than what we see of them
three years of weekly hangouts while carrying this says a lot about who you are in a friendship
the friendship we have now is different from the one before. I had to grieve the first one to actually have the second
what she told you might not even represent who she is now. people genuinely change. three years is real time
what would it look like to have an honest conversation about it? not accusatory. just honest.
she gave you her truth and it cost her nothing. you've been carrying it for three years. that math doesn't add up
somewhere between who she was and who you thought she was is who she actually is. you're the only one who sees all three
who we are in our worst or weakest moments is part of who we are. not all of it. part of it.
love that survives full information is more honest than love built on curated versions of each other
friendships can survive honesty about the things that changed us. sometimes they come out stronger on the other side
you don't have to tell her it shifted things. but figure out if it still matters to you or if it's fading
at some point you have to decide if you're in this friendship or performing it. only you know which one this is
whatever you decide — to say something or keep carrying it — I hope you make the choice that leaves you lighter
you should tell her it changed something. not as accusation. as truth. the friendship can hold it or it can't
I keep wondering what she would say if you told her it's been sitting with you. has that conversation ever crossed your mind
I'm not saying break the confidence. I'm saying you're allowed to tell her that it affected you. those are separate
you've chosen her every week for three years. that's not nothing. that's love with its eyes open.
